transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (Zenith Infra), Sofia Alvarez (Zenith ML), Marco Ruiz (Zenith Platform), Nora Patel (Zenith Security)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for blocking time. quick agenda — walk through the two watchdog incidents you sent over, dig into kv cache + batching behavior, and decide on next steps. priya will lead the repro plan.
[00:14] Liam: thanks jordan. yeah, we've seen two pretty noisy incidents over the last three weeks, both on our private deployment in ap-southeast-2, 8xA100s. first was july 24th and then august 1st. results look like device reset, then a cascade of 503s.
[00:29] Priya: hi, everyone. quick clarifying q — the traces you uploaded, are they aggregated traces from the router or raw per-worker nvml traces?
[00:36] Marco: most are from our sidecar router and the system logs; we couldn't pull nvml by default because of our security posture, so we attached what we could — traces, systemd-journald snippets, and one driver core dump.
[00:50] Sofia: and to be explicit — the model is our in-house finetuned chat model, converted to a quantized int8 profile using q4_0 tooling. we do long prefix messages frequently, many times 1.2–1.8k tokens of context.
[01:04] Priya: okay that helps a lot. long prefix plus quantized weights is a common stress pattern especially if kvcache isn't capped.
[01:12] Nora: quick security note — we can't share raw nvml logs without redaction, that's why there was a delay. happy to provide redacted artifacts.
[01:20] Jordan: noted. priya, can you summarise the hypothesis before we look at logs?
[01:23] Priya: sure. hypothesis A: kv cache grows with prefixes because of conversation history, combined with batching spikes that co-locate several large prefixes into one GPU, pushing transient memory over the driver watchdog threshold. Hypothesis B: quantization path produces different memory allocation patterns and calls a less-optimized CUDA kernel that has longer launch latencies — turning short spikes into watchdog-triggering stalls. Also we saw evidence of retries happening quickly without exponential backoff, which amplifies pressure.
[01:51] Liam: one of our observations is that retries were handled by the router almost immediately — like three attempts in under a second. that's because our router default is eager retry on worker failure.
[02:02] Priya: that explains the amplification. multiple workers get hit when the first one resets, router retries send new work into remaining workers, they see the same heavy prefixes and memory gets hammered.
[02:14] Marco: in our config we had a high batching target — peak batch size 64 for throughput — we tuned that for cost. is there a recommendation to reduce that?
[02:23] Priya: yes, adaptive batch sizing that considers prefix token counts is key. small batches for large prefixes. also enforce a per-request wss memory cap.
[02:33] Sofia: curious — you mentioned quantization kernel differences. do you have specifics on which kernels or cuBLAS/attention implementations might be slower?
[02:40] Priya: there's a mix — the int8 path often uses lower-precision GEMMs and custom kernels. on some CUDA driver revisions there's a path that falls back to a non-streamed kernel which serializes more work on launch. that increases latency for each op and if a kernel hold time crosses the watchdog threshold (usually a few hundred ms on driver settings) the OS resets the GPU.
[03:03] Jordan: do we know the driver version for the incidents?
[03:06] Liam: one incident was on driver 535.xx and the other on 534.xx — i don't recall exact patch.
[03:12] Priya: okay that's in the range where we've seen a couple of regressions. we'll correlate exact patch levels when you provide the nvml dumps.
[03:19] [03:20] -- brief crosstalk --
[03:22] Marco: what about kernel preemption settings? our ops team has preemption disabled to avoid context-switching overhead. could that make things worse?
[03:29] Priya: yes — disabling preemption can increase worst-case kernel run time. preemption helps the driver kill or preempt long-running kernels before the watchdog expires. but preemption can interact badly with concurrent kernels and reduce throughput, so it's a trade.
[03:41] Sofia: can Redwood's runtime detect prefix-heavy batches and split them automatically?
[03:45] Priya: we have heuristics in the serving runtime — we can enable prefix-aware batching where the router tags requests with prefix length and the batcher enforces max total prefix tokens per batch. in hosted mode we enable this by default for certain models.
[03:58] Liam: in our private deployment we didn't enable that because we didn't see it in the initial rollout docs.
[04:03] Jordan: we'll include recommended config flags for private deploys. priya, walk us through the log snippets.
[04:08] Priya: sure. looking at the journal provided — timestamp 2026-07-24T03:22:11 — we see a sequence: sustained allocation spikes, then a CUDA watchdog timeout (error: CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT), then NVML reports device reset. right after, router entries show immediate retry attempts for the requests in flight.
[04:31] [04:32] Sofia: that matches the user-facing errors — users saw 500 then 503 repeatedly for a few minutes.
[04:36] Priya: there's also a pattern where ephemeral CUDA memory fragmentation increases over time under sustained prefixes — likely due to per-token KV allocations that aren't consolidated. the quantized backend seems to use different allocation patterns which are less friendly to the allocator.
[04:53] Liam: is that the kvcache per-layer issue we saw in earlier redwood notes? like duplicated kv snapshots across micro-batches?
[04:59] Priya: yes, in some configurations multiple micro-batches can create duplicate KV references, especially if the batcher replicates prefix state rather than referencing a shared prefix buffer. that's an expensive copy.
[05:09] Marco: so architecture-wise, is the fix on routing/batching side or runtime allocator side?
[05:14] Priya: both. short-term mitigations: router/backoff changes (increase backoff jitter, add rate-limited retries), batcher changes (prefix-aware batch caps), and runtime changes (stricter per-request memory limits, better KV sharing and deferred allocations). long-term: kernel selection improvements and working with driver vendors on regression fixes.
[05:33] Nora: from security — any of these mitigations need to avoid changing telemetry that we can't share. also we need a retained audit trail. can Redwood accept redacted nvml logs in the private deployment scenario?
[05:44] Jordan: yes, we can accept redacted dumps. our SEs can work with sanitized stacks; we also have a private agent that runs inside customer VPC to collect diagnostic artifacts securely.
[05:56] Liam: that's good. the agent approach might be necessary.
[05:58] [06:00] -- timestamp --
[06:02] Priya: i ran a quick internal repro on a similar model and observed that combining three long-prefix requests in one batch produced a transient allocation 1.8x higher vs single request. when quantized kernels used non-streamed fallback the per-kernel wall time jumped from ~30ms to ~420ms which is a problem.
[06:23] Sofia: wow 420ms — that will trip watchdogs. is the non-streamed fallback deterministic?
[06:27] Priya: it's influenced by driver and lib versions and sometimes by internal workspace sizes; it's not deterministic across all loads.
[06:34] Jordan: for the repro plan — priya recommended a focused trace with controlled batches, right?
[06:38] Priya: yes: 1) replay three representative sessions with long prefixes into a staging cluster (8xA100 matching zenith), 2) enable verbose nvml tracing and per-worker allocator debug, 3) try different driver versions (534.x vs 536.x) and observe kernel path selection.
[06:55] Marco: we can do that but testing different drivers in staging is time-consuming. can we try kernel-level mitigations without driver changes?
[07:03] Priya: yes — runtime can force different kernel choices or disable a specific optimized kernel to force a more stream-friendly path; sometimes that reduces throughput slightly but avoids long running kernels. also we can cap batch size for long-prefix traffic, or set per-request memory cap to cause early rejection rather than letting the device hit the watchdog.
[07:22] Liam: about early rejection — how do we avoid a bad UX? We could return a graceful degrade like shorter context or reroute to CPU fallback.
[07:30] Priya: exactly. we have a graceful-fallback policy: detect prefix above threshold -> route to quantized CPU fallback (higher latency, lower cost) or warn the client to trim prefix. customers prefer routing to dedicated CPU instances for rare heavy requests rather than risking a full node reset.
[07:46] Sofia: curious about retry semantics again. if the router does exponential backoff with increasing delays, does that meaningfully reduce amplified pressure?
[07:53] Priya: yes, especially if combined with circuit-breaking: open the circuit for a worker if multiple resets happen in short window and spread new requests to healthy workers or reduce concurrency.
[08:03] Marco: do you have a recommended default backoff config?
[08:06] Priya: we recommend start backoff 200ms, multiplier 2, max 5s, and a retry cap of 3 attempts total. plus jitter to prevent thundering herd.
[08:16] Jordan: there was a question in the ticket about whether reduced batch target to 32 would be enough. thoughts?
[08:21] Priya: lowering to 32 helps but you must consider prefix tokens per batch. a batch of 32 small requests is fine; a batch of 8 requests with 2k tokens each is not. the metric to watch is total active kb of kv state per GPU. cap that rather than just request count.
[08:38] Liam: ok — we'll create a metric for kv-state-by-gpu.
[08:41] [08:42] -- pauses for a second --
[08:44] Sofia: one more thing — our models have per-layer KV caching that sometimes duplicates when we do micro-batching for throughput. is there a way to share layer KV on the runtime?
[08:53] Priya: yes, runtime-level shared KV buffers are in our roadmap; in some deployments we already have an opt-in shared-prefix mode where the loader pins prefix buffers and references them across micro-batches instead of copying. it's slightly more complex memory management but dramatically reduces duplication. we can enable that for your staging repro.
[09:09] Marco: excellent. sounds like a plan.
[09:12] Priya: operational debugging checklist I propose: 1) collect driver and CUDA versions, nvml logs, dmesg, kernel ring buffer; 2) capture router retry logs and timestamps; 3) capture per-worker allocator metrics (resident set, peak allocs, fragmentation).
[09:31] Liam: on the private deployment, we need instructions for how the Redwood agent collects nvml logs without sending raw PII or secret keys.
[09:38] Jordan: we'll provide the agent with an opt-in script and a signed config. security will review.
[09:43] Nora: please include an explanation of what the agent collects and how it stores logs, retention, and who at Redwood can access them.
[09:50] Jordan: noted. we'll include an appendix.
[09:53] [10:00] -- mid-call recap --
[10:02] Jordan: recap: 1) priya will run repro in Redwood infra and try kernel forcing and batch caps; 2) zenith will supply redacted NVML + dmesg by next wed; 3) jordan sends pilot pricing and SOC2 docs. any other points?
[10:16] Sofia: could you also show what the fallback to CPU looks like latency-wise in the repro?
[10:20] Priya: yes we'll include a CPU fallback run; typically latency jumps X4–X6 depending on model size but avoids resets.
[10:27] Liam: we will also test router backoff changes in staging.
[10:30] Marco: how soon can priya start on the repro?
[10:33] Priya: i can start tomorrow; will need the sample traces and a staging account to mirror your deployment.
[10:39] Jordan: we'll send the staging invitation and minimal runbook after the call.
[10:43] [10:50] -- deeper technical Q/A --
[10:51] Sofia: you mentioned fragmentation — any quick mitigation other than reboot?
[10:56] Priya: we can do periodic worker-level memory compaction by restarting the process or preallocating bigger arenas to avoid many small allocations. another trick is to use pooled allocators tuned for the kernel workspace sizes. these are config knobs in the runtime.
[11:11] Liam: does quantization increase fragmentation risk vs fp16?
[11:14] Priya: yes, because quantized kernels sometimes request different workspace shapes and allocate more transient buffers per-layer leading to more scatter allocations. fp16 tends to be more regular.
[11:23] Nora: from compliance perspective — if you propose automatic batch-splitting, we need to ensure logs still map to request ids for auditing.
[11:30] Jordan: yes — batch-split keeps original request ids and we log the mapping; that will be in the runbook.
[11:36] Marco: any final recommendations on driver versions?
[11:39] Priya: avoid driver ver X where we saw the known regression (we'll point to exact patch in the follow-up). test 534.x vs 536.x in staging.
[11:49] Sofia: ok.
[11:50] [11:52] -- closing and next steps --
[11:53] Jordan: thanks all. priya, once you have initial repro notes, can you include an experiment matrix: batch sizes, prefix caps, driver versions, kernel forcing flags?
[12:02] Priya: yes I'll paste the matrix to the ticket.
[12:05] Jordan: and zenith team — please upload the redacted diagnostic artifacts to the shared S3 link.
[12:11] Liam: will do. thanks everyone.
[12:13] Sofia: thank you.
[12:15] Nora: thanks.
